title: Master Tara Singh
hookLine: a schoolteacher who led the Akalis for decades

cards: Some nicknames outlive the job. A coach is still Coach at the grocery store years after the last game. In Punjab, one Sikh leader kept a classroom title long after he'd left the classroom.
Not General, not President, not Sardar. Master, as in schoolmaster. He led marches, negotiated with governments and went to jail, and people kept calling him the teacher.

teach.b: Tara Singh was born into a Hindu family, and as a young man he chose the Sikh path and took amrit, the Khalsa initiation.
That's how his biographers tell it, and it shaped him: he came to the panth by choice, and defended it for the rest of his life.

He studied at Khalsa College in Amritsar, which came up earlier in this block, then became a teacher and a headmaster at a Khalsa school. Teaching, for him, wasn't a stop on the way to something else.
It was how he understood leading: explain, persuade, keep the students together.
When the gurdwara reform movement rose, he joined it and soon stood among its leaders.
He led the Akali Dal and the SGPC for many years, through the reform campaigns and later through the hard years around the partition of Punjab. He was jailed more than once.
Sikhs still argue about his politics and his decisions, and historians weigh them differently; that argument isn't settled here. But friends and critics alike remember the name he kept.
The Asa di Var opens, at Ang 462 of the Guru Granth Sahib, with Guru Nanak saying he is a sacrifice to his Guru a hundred times a day, the Guru who made angels out of humans without delay.
In Gurbani that gratitude belongs to the Guru. But it colors the way Sikhs speak of anyone who teaches, and helps explain why a classroom title became a name of respect for a lifetime.

how: Master Tara Singh is remembered among Sikhs as a leader of the Akali Dal and the SGPC through the reform years and after; his life and decisions are discussed in Sikh histories, and his name is on schools and public places in Punjab.

games.q: you're a headmaster at a Khalsa school when the gurdwara reform movement rises. what does Tara Singh do?
o: stay in the classroom and keep out of it.
join the movement and become one of its leaders.
games.why: he joined the reform movement and led the Akalis for many years, and people never stopped calling him Master.

practice: Bring to mind one teacher who changed something in you: a schoolteacher, a coach, a grandparent, a boss, someone at the gurdwara who showed you how to sit with the Guru Granth Sahib.
Picture their face and voice, remember one thing they said that stayed, and let a little gratitude come with each breath out. If you pray, let it come with Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: Tara Singh, a schoolteacher and headmaster who led the Akalis for decades, and was called by the teacher's title, Master, all his life. Today's word.

orig.note: master, the English schoolmaster's title, carried into Punjabi as a name of respect.

carryVoice: Your line: the teacher-leader. Sometimes a title is how people say thank you for years. See you tomorrow.
